heading: Cold open
narration: Its name promises a monster from hell, but the animal is about a foot long.

heading: Cold open
narration: The vampire squid is a small, soft deep-sea cephalopod, about 30 centimetres long, dark reddish-brown to black, with eight arms joined by a web of skin, a pair of fins that stick out like ears, and eyes that, relative to its body, are often described as the largest of any animal.

heading: Cold open
narration: That length is the figure MBARI gives for adults. The description is easy to state.

heading: Cold open
narration: It does not explain why the picture took so long to get right.

heading: Cold open
narration: For most of this animal's scientific history, the people describing it had only seen it dead, crushed and faded at the bottom of a net.

heading: Cold open
narration: Its adult length is the easy part. Its shape, its colour and even what it eats were first read from damaged evidence and corrected later.

heading: Title card
narration: What does a vampire squid look like?

heading: Its body is a cloak, not a torpedo
narration: Start with the body plan. A true squid is a streamlined tube built for speed.

heading: Its body is a cloak, not a torpedo
narration: The vampire squid is closer to a small umbrella. Its body, called the mantle, is short and rounded, and eight arms hang from it.

heading: Its body is a cloak, not a torpedo
narration: Those arms do not move freely the way an octopus's arms do.

heading: Its body is a cloak, not a torpedo
narration: A sheet of skin, the web, runs between them almost to their tips.

heading: Its body is a cloak, not a torpedo
narration: When the arms spread, the animal looks like it is holding open a dark cape.

heading: Its body is a cloak, not a torpedo
narration: The vampire part of the name comes from that cape. Two fins sit on the mantle, one on each side, and from the front they look like ears. The animal flaps them to swim, and it swims slowly.

heading: Its body is a cloak, not a torpedo
narration: Turn the cape inside out and the inner surface looks fierce. Rows of pale, pointed structures run down each arm.

heading: Its body is a cloak, not a torpedo
narration: They look like fangs, and footage is often edited to make them seem like fangs.

heading: Its body is a cloak, not a torpedo
narration: They are cirri, which are soft fleshy spines, not teeth or hooks.

heading: Its body is a cloak, not a torpedo
narration: They do not bite and they do not grip. This is the first place where what the animal looks like and what it actually is come apart.

heading: Its body is a cloak, not a torpedo
narration: A still photograph of the inner web reads as armour. Video of the living animal shows the cirri as flexible, almost limp.

heading: Its body is a cloak, not a torpedo
narration: Their likely role is sensory. The word likely matters. That role is an inference from structure and behaviour. Nobody has measured it as a function.

heading: Its body is a cloak, not a torpedo
narration: Then there are the eyes. The animal is roughly a foot long, and its eyes are large enough to dominate its head.

heading: Its body is a cloak, not a torpedo
narration: Relative to body size, they are often described as the largest of any animal.

heading: Its body is a cloak, not a torpedo
narration: Their colour on film depends on the lighting. Under the white lamps of an underwater camera they can look blue or red.

heading: Its body is a cloak, not a torpedo
narration: The skin behaves the same way. The animal is usually described as black to reddish-brown, but the colour you see in any image partly depends on the lamp.

heading: Its body is a cloak, not a torpedo
narration: Deep water is dark. Every colour photograph of a deep animal records light that the camera itself brought down.

heading: The first pictures came from wrecked specimens
narration: Here is how the animal was first known. For a long time, deep-sea animals were brought up in trawl nets towed behind ships.

args.title: How the animal was first known

heading: The first pictures came from wrecked specimens
narration: A net is a good way to learn that something exists. It is a poor way to learn what that thing looks like.

heading: The first pictures came from wrecked specimens
narration: The vampire squid is soft and gelatinous. A body like that, dragged up from the deep in a net full of other animals, arrives torn, collapsed and drained of colour.

args.title: How the animal was first known

heading: The first pictures came from wrecked specimens
narration: Each specimen was then preserved in a jar, drawn and described, and every step added distance from the living animal.

heading: The first pictures came from wrecked specimens
narration: Preservative changes colour and shrinks tissue. A collapsed web gives no hint of how the animal holds itself.

args.title: How the animal was first known

heading: The first pictures came from wrecked specimens
narration: What changed the picture was going down to the animal instead of pulling it up.

heading: The first pictures came from wrecked specimens
narration: MBARI, working off the coast of California, has spent decades sending remotely operated vehicles into the deep water column.

heading: The first pictures came from wrecked specimens
narration: These are robots tethered to a ship and fitted with high-definition cameras.

heading: The first pictures came from wrecked specimens
narration: A camera records the animal undamaged and in its own posture. It records minutes of movement instead of a single frozen moment.

heading: The first pictures came from wrecked specimens
narration: Most modern descriptions rest on this kind of evidence. A confident, detailed account of how a vampire squid looks usually comes from video, checked against preserved specimens. Specimens alone did not produce it.

heading: The first pictures came from wrecked specimens
narration: No single source draws the whole picture. MBARI's video records shape and behaviour.

heading: The first pictures came from wrecked specimens
narration: Preserved specimens in natural history collections let anatomists dissect and measure the parts that video cannot reach.

heading: The first pictures came from wrecked specimens
narration: The broader surveys of the deep, from bodies such as NOAA Ocean Exploration and Smithsonian Ocean, place the animal within the wider ecosystem.

heading: The first pictures came from wrecked specimens
narration: Each kind of evidence covers a weakness in another. Video cannot show stomach contents.

heading: The first pictures came from wrecked specimens
narration: A jar cannot show posture. The modern description is trustworthy because these sources agree.

heading: Producer POV
narration: The disturbing part isn't that mistakes happen. It's how resistant institutions become once careers, textbooks and reputations depend on the old answer staying true.

args.text: The disturbing part isn't that mistakes happen. It's how resistant institutions become once careers, textbooks and reputations depend on the old answer staying true.

heading: It is not a squid, and not an octopus either
narration: Despite the name, it is not a squid. It is not an octopus either.

heading: It is not a squid, and not an octopus either
narration: Its common name calls it a squid, but the first scientific description placed it among the octopuses, and later work moved it again.

heading: It is not a squid, and not an octopus either
narration: It shares features with both groups. Like an octopus, it has eight webbed arms.

heading: It is not a squid, and not an octopus either
narration: Unlike an octopus, it also carries two extra filaments tucked into pockets.

heading: It is not a squid, and not an octopus either
narration: Today it sits in its own order, Vampyromorphida, and it is the only living species in that order.

heading: It is not a squid, and not an octopus either
narration: Its formal name, Vampyroteuthis infernalis, translates roughly as vampire squid from hell. A name records first impressions. It is not a description.

heading: It is not a squid, and not an octopus either
narration: The classification has a second history. Early specimens differed from one another because of damage, age and preservation.

heading: It is not a squid, and not an octopus either
narration: Several were described under different names before researchers recognised them as a single species.

heading: It is not a squid, and not an octopus either
narration: The fins show why this happened. Young vampire squid pass through a stage with two pairs of fins, and adults have one pair.

heading: It is not a squid, and not an octopus either
narration: A biologist working from a few jars could reasonably conclude that a juvenile and an adult were different animals.

heading: It is not a squid, and not an octopus either
narration: A better argument did not fix the error. More specimens did, and eventually so did watching living animals.

heading: Two filaments explain the strangest part of its outline
narration: The feeding filaments are easy to miss in a photograph, because the animal can pull them back into pockets between its arms.

heading: Two filaments explain the strangest part of its outline
narration: Extended, they can reach much farther than the length of its body.

heading: Two filaments explain the strangest part of its outline
narration: For a long time, nobody was sure what they were for. The answer came from research at MBARI, which combined video of living animals with the stomach contents of preserved specimens.

heading: Two filaments explain the strangest part of its outline
narration: Together, these showed that the vampire squid uses its filaments for collecting marine snow.

heading: Two filaments explain the strangest part of its outline
narration: Marine snow is the steady fall of dead plankton, faecal pellets and other debris sinking from above.

heading: Two filaments explain the strangest part of its outline
narration: The animal gathers this material in mucus and passes it to its mouth with its arms.

heading: Two filaments explain the strangest part of its outline
narration: That finding is why the fearsome look misleads. Most cephalopods are predators.

heading: Two filaments explain the strangest part of its outline
narration: Judged by what is in its stomach and what it is seen doing, the vampire squid is a collector.

heading: Two filaments explain the strangest part of its outline
narration: It is not hunting live prey. It drifts, lets the filaments trail, and waits for food to settle onto them.

heading: Two filaments explain the strangest part of its outline
narration: The cape, the cirri and the dark colour look like a hunter's equipment.

heading: Two filaments explain the strangest part of its outline
narration: They belong to an animal that lives on the ocean's sinking leftovers.

heading: Light is part of how it looks
narration: Where it lives, sunlight has almost disappeared. Water absorbs red light first, close to the surface.

heading: Light is part of how it looks
narration: At the depths this animal prefers, only a faint trace of blue remains.

heading: Light is part of how it looks
narration: That is too little light for most of the colours in photographs to exist naturally.

heading: Light is part of how it looks
narration: In that blue gloom, a dark red or black body is effectively invisible.

heading: Light is part of how it looks
narration: An animal coloured this way is not displaying a colour. It is removing one. The light it does display is its own.

heading: Light is part of how it looks
narration: The vampire squid is covered in light organs called photophores, and the tips of its arms can glow.

heading: Light is part of how it looks
narration: When it is disturbed, it can do something unusual. Other cephalopods release a cloud of dark ink.

heading: Light is part of how it looks
narration: The vampire squid can instead release a sticky cloud of glowing particles from its arm tips.

heading: Light is part of how it looks
narration: The cloud lingers in the water while the animal moves away. In another defensive display, it pulls its webbed arms up and back over its body and turns itself inside out, so that the cirri face outward.

heading: Light is part of how it looks
narration: Researchers sometimes call this the pineapple posture. In that position the animal looks like a spiny ball, and the dark cape disappears entirely.

heading: Its habitat explains its build
narration: MBARI reports that the vampire squid most often lives between about 600 and 900 metres deep.

heading: Its habitat explains its build
narration: That is in the twilight zone, in a layer called the oxygen minimum zone, where the water holds very little oxygen.

heading: Its habitat explains its build
narration: Few predators can stay there for long. The vampire squid's body suits that setting.

heading: Its habitat explains its build
narration: Its tissues are soft and watery, its muscles are weak compared with a squid's, and its metabolism is slow.

heading: Its habitat explains its build
narration: An animal that spends little energy can survive on little oxygen and little food.

heading: Its habitat explains its build
narration: That physical logic explains its appearance. A soft, slow, drifting body is the shape of a life lived on a tight budget.

heading: What to notice in the edit
narration: When you watch footage of this animal, look for three things. First, look at the lighting, because the camera carried down every colour you see.

heading: What to notice in the edit
narration: Second, check whether the animal is swimming with its fins, drifting with its filaments out, or curled into its defensive posture.

heading: What to notice in the edit
narration: Those are different shapes of the same body. Third, look at the scale.

heading: What to notice in the edit
narration: On a large screen with no reference object nearby, a 30-centimetre animal can look enormous. The footage is accurate. Your sense of its size is not.

heading: Evidence limit
narration: Here is what the evidence settles and what it leaves open. The posture and behaviour on video, and the diet from stomach contents, are well supported.

heading: Evidence limit
narration: But most video of living vampire squid comes from a few regions where research vehicles dive regularly, and many observations come from off California.

heading: Evidence limit
narration: The animal lives across tropical and temperate oceans, so our picture of its behaviour comes from a narrow slice of a wide range.

heading: Evidence limit
narration: Every image is artificially lit, so its colour under natural light is inferred, not observed.

heading: Evidence limit
narration: The purpose of the cirri is inferred from their structure. Other basic facts remain poorly established, including how long an individual lives, how often it breeds and how many there are. Estimates vary, and the published evidence is thin.

heading: Closing
narration: So the vampire squid is a small, dark, soft animal with a webbed cape, ear-like fins and very large eyes.

heading: Closing
narration: The more interesting part is how scientists earned that picture: first from wrecked bodies in jars, then from cameras that went down to meet the animal where it lives.
